newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banker warns nations to focus on EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: German banker warns nations to focus on EMU goal.

text.p: Europe should not lose sight of the greater goal of European integration as nations rush to get their finances in order to join the planned currency union, a senior German banking official warned on Friday.

Martin Kohlhaussen, chief executive at Germany's third largest commercial bank Commerzbank AG, told the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt that monetary union and political integration should "unite and strengthen Europe".
But he added: "We run the risk of losing sight of the overriding goal for all the details."

He worried that some nations' last minute efforts to whip their finances into shape in order to be among the first group of nations to join the currency union as well as the row over the so-called stability pact to ensure permanent fiscal austerity were "disturbing signs".

As the planned monetary union has not yet earned the trust of citizens and markets, Kohlhaussen said those pushing the project forward "should be careful not to sow the seeds of mistrust or confirm existing prejudices."

At the same time Kohlhaussen also said the monetary union cannot be all things to all people, saying the union "can't secure price stability and function as an 'exchange-rate-union' that protects industry from currency fluctuations which distort competition".
Exchange rate fluctuations are most likely to occur in nations not ready to take part in the currency union, which is committed to maintaining price stability, Kohlhaussen said.
The union also cannot be a "transfer-union", Kohlhaussen said, warning against restributing wealth between regions.
Instead the currency union will increase competition, forcing nations to adjust quickly to new conditions, he said.
Europe's currency union is scheduled to begin on January 1, 1999 with those nations meeting strict entry requirements on budget deficits, debt, inflation rates and exchange rates.
